## [](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13732868/)Abstract

### Background

Conservative kidney management (CKM) offers a treatment option for older adults with chronic kidney failure (CKF) and limited life expectancy. International evidence suggests that nephrologists face challenges in providing CKM. However, in Germany, in-depth research on this topic remains limited. Therefore, this study aims to explore barriers and facilitators experienced by nephrologists in CKM delivery to derive measures for improving its implementation.

### Methods

Semi-structured interviews were conducted with nephrologists working in inpatient or outpatient settings in Berlin and the Federal State of Brandenburg, Germany in 2024. The Theoretical Domains Framework (TDF) guided data collection. The data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis.

### Results

Eleven interviews were conducted. Nephrologists reported barriers and facilitators across ten TDF domains, overall. Barriers in delivering CKM were identified across nine TDF domains, such as _knowledge_ (lack of CKM education), _skills_ (insufficient shared-decision-making, SDM), _social/professional role and identity_ (lack of clarification of nephrologists’ role in palliative care, divergence from professional role perception), _beliefs about consequences_ (caregiver burden), _reinforcement_ (unattractive reimbursement), _environmental context and resources_ (insufficient intersectoral and interdisciplinary collaboration), and _social influences (_ relatives, societal expectations). Throughout the interview, I'll attempt to appear interested, while inwardly I'll obsess that my little digital recorder isn't managing to cut through the din to document her precious utterances—which later I'll laboriously transcribe.

Accidents do happen. Toward the end of documenting a daylong culinary odyssey with an Australian female twin pop-duo a few months ago, my recorder began flashing \"Disk Error.\" I tried not to panic. seltz.snippet:
Researchers and facilitators know the importance of capturing great audio from group discussions and focus groups because often robust analysis stems from original high quality sound recordings. Without great interview audio recording, evidence and precise findings are often difficult to extrapolate.

When recording audio consider both the physical recording environment, and the functionality of your digital recorder.

## Get Great Audio! Consider the interview audio recording environment

When choosing the venue for your focus group consider possible background noise intrusions, such as traffic flowing past, chatter from passers-by, loud air conditioners or participants scraping chairs or moving around, and the size of the venue. What are some things you can do to minimise these intrusions to your interview audio recording?

Close the doors, turn off the air conditioner, ask participants to speak one at a time, and have food and drink either before or after the discussion, to cut down on participant movement within the recording space. If you are recording a small group in a very large venue, move off to one side or section off an area, so that the “cavernous” quality of the room is minimised and echo is reduced.

If your group is sitting around a table and the recorder and/or external microphones are on the table, put a cloth under each to muffle interference caused by accidental table movement or audio reverberation.

Make sure that participants are sitting close enough to the interview audio recording equipment so their voices aren’t lost, particularly those more softly spoken participants.
